title: The times that open
hook: in prostration, the last third of the night, between adhan and iqamah, while fasting

segments.voice: Yesterday: asking for someone absent, and the angel who answers. Your line was and the same for you. Whose name crossed your mind, and did you wish them one good thing? Day one hundred thirty-five.
screen: `ASKING FOR SOMEONE ABSENT — AND THE SAME FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Every office has one. The manager whose door is technically always open, but everyone knows the good time to ask is Friday afternoon, after lunch, when things are calm. Timing isn't everything, but it's something. This week we've said du'a can be made anywhere, any time, in any words. That's still true. The door is never locked. But the hadith collections also name certain moments when the door is described as especially wide open. Moments to save your biggest asks for. Today: the times that open.
screen: `THE DOOR IS ALWAYS OPEN.` → `BUT SOME MOMENTS ARE WIDER.` → `SAVE YOUR BIGGEST ASKS.`

segments.voice: Here are four of them. The first you already know from day one hundred five: in prostration. Sahih Muslim reports that the closest a servant is to his Lord is while prostrating, so ask much there. Forehead on the floor, and many Muslims pour their private requests into those few seconds, silently, in their own words. The second is the last third of the night. Bukhari and Muslim report that every night, when the last third remains, our Lord descends to the nearest heaven and says: who is calling on Me, that I may answer? Who is asking of Me, that I may give? Who is seeking forgiveness, that I may forgive? Scholars have long differed on how to understand that descent; many simply accept it without asking how. Either way, the picture is of the whole sky listening while almost everyone is asleep. It's why some Muslims set an alarm for an hour before dawn. The third is small and ordinary: between the adhan and the iqamah, the call to prayer and the call to stand. Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi report that a du'a made in that gap is not turned back. Those few minutes when people are waiting in the mosque, checking the time, are described as an open door. The fourth is while fasting. Tirmidhi reports that the fasting person's du'a is among those not rejected, and many Muslims make du'a just before breaking the fast at sunset. There are others: part of Friday, while traveling, when it rains. But notice what these four share. Lowered. Awake while others sleep. Waiting. Hungry. Moments when a person is a little emptier than usual.
screen: `FIRST: IN PROSTRATION.` · `THE LAST THIRD OF THE NIGHT.` · `BETWEEN THE ADHAN AND THE IQAMAH.` · `WHILE FASTING.` · then, large: `A LITTLE EMPTIER THAN USUAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one time this week. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Run through the four in your mind. Face on the floor. The quiet hour before dawn. The waiting minutes before a prayer. The last minute of an empty stomach. Which one could you actually reach this week? Choose one. Picture it: where you'll be, what the room looks like. If you pray, decide now what you'll ask for when you get there. If not, decide what you'll sit quietly with. The bell holds the time.
The times that open. Prostration, the last third of the night, the gap between the adhan and the iqamah, and the fast: moments the hadith describe as especially open to du'a. Today's word.
Your line: knock at the open door. Put the time you chose into your calendar or set an alarm for it now, and keep one question ready for when it comes. Day one hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Many Muslims save their most important du'a for prostration, the last third of the night, the time between the adhan and the iqamah, and the moments before breaking a fast.

trapdoor: what you thought: you can pray whenever, so timing doesn't matter.
what it means: the door is always open, but the hadith name moments when it's wider.
what a scholar hears: Muslim 482 on sujud; the nuzul hadith (Bukhari 1145, Muslim 758) and its long debate; Abu Dawud 521; Tirmidhi 3598.
